stem: A high-volume ticket router classifies requests under a strict latency budget; the smallest model already clears the accuracy bar. A new certification mandate requires each classification carry an auditable rationale, not just a pass/fail score. Select the correct move.

opts.t: Move to a higher-capability model; only richer reasoning can produce the auditable rationale the certification mandate requires.
Keep the smallest model, since it already clears the accuracy bar the team benchmarked against.
Keep the smallest model, and add periodic manual audits of a sample of its classifications for compliance review.
Fine-tune the smallest model on tagged examples, without first testing whether a larger model already produces the required rationale.

whyRight: The mandate requires an auditable rationale for every classification, not just an accuracy score — a requirement the accuracy-bar test cannot verify. A bounded, high-volume classifier answers speed and cost; explaining its own reasoning at the standard a certification audit demands calls for a higher-capability model.

whyWrong.B: Clearing the accuracy bar answers a different question than the mandate asks; the stem states the requirement is an auditable rationale, which a pass/fail benchmark score does not provide.
whyWrong.C: Auditing a sample after the fact only detects gaps; the mandate requires an auditable rationale for every classification, produced up front, not discovered after deployment.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning is an expensive lever aimed at accuracy, not at producing the auditable rationale the mandate specifically requires; it doesn't test whether a larger model already meets it.

t1Clause: A new certification mandate requires each classification carry an auditable rationale, not just a pass/fail score.
lessonKey: auditable can capability certification higher mandate model move only produce rationale reasoning requires richer

stem: A system prompt already blocks any refund mention outside business hours. A compliance officer holds written approval for after-hours refund reviews during fraud investigations; the boundary must hold for every other case before an audit. What should the team do?

opts.t: Reword the guardrail's refusal language to sound stricter, without changing what triggers it or where it lives.
Remove the guardrail and instead log every refund request for a reviewer to check afterward.
Configure the fraud-investigation exception as an environment variable the operations team can toggle during audits.
Add a scoped exception for the approved fraud-investigation case directly into the system-prompt guardrail, leaving the boundary intact elsewhere.

whyRight: The guardrail's location is already correct — the fix is to narrow what it blocks, not where it lives. Writing the approved fraud-investigation exception directly into the system-prompt guardrail preserves its authority everywhere else while accommodating the one case leadership has actually authorized.

whyWrong.A: Rewording the refusal language changes nothing about which requests it blocks; the approved fraud-investigation case would still be refused exactly as before.
whyWrong.B: Removing the guardrail drops preventive enforcement entirely; a reviewer checking logs afterward cannot stop an unauthorized refund before it happens.
whyWrong.C: Environment variables are deploy-time infrastructure configuration; they never reach the model, so the exception would have no effect on its actual behavior.

t1Clause: a compliance officer holds written approval for an after-hours fraud-investigation exception
lessonKey: add approved boundary case directly elsewhere exception fraud guardrail intact into investigation leaving prompt scoped system

stem: A high-volume support-formatting feature inconsistently applies one output format despite clear instructions, with one sprint left before launch. A colleague proposes adding twelve examples covering formats the model already handles correctly. What should the team do?

opts.t: Add the twelve examples as proposed; broader example coverage reinforces the model's formatting behavior overall.
Rewrite the system prompt instructions to state the formatting rule in even more explicit language.
Replace the twelve examples with four to six examples targeted at the exact case that keeps failing.
Add all twelve examples now for thoroughness, and add targeted ones later only if the case still fails.

whyRight: The failure is a targeting problem, not a volume problem. Twelve examples of cases the model already handles correctly never touch the one case still failing; four to six examples built from that exact failing case fix the ambiguity examples exist to resolve.

whyWrong.A: More examples do not help if they cover cases the model already gets right; the twelve as proposed never address the one case that keeps failing.
whyWrong.B: Instructions have already failed to produce consistent output; rewording them again doesn't fix a precision problem that targeted examples are built to solve.
whyWrong.D: Adding volume now and targeting later reverses the order that fixes the failure; the twelve broad examples spend the sprint's budget without touching the actual case.

t1Clause: covering formats the model already handles correctly

stem: A support agent's per-turn latency and token cost climb steadily as a conversation passes fifty turns, even though each response stays about the same length, threatening a per-session cost cap. An engineer blames Claude's memory buffer filling up internally. What is the actual cause?

opts.t: The context window is being exceeded this early in a fifty-turn conversation.
Claude retains an internal memory buffer across calls that grows heavier with each additional turn.
The model is generating progressively longer, more detailed responses as the conversation continues.
The application resends the full conversation history on every call, so token volume grows with each additional turn.

whyRight: The API is stateless: nothing about the conversation persists on Claude's side between calls. Every request must resend the complete history, so as a conversation lengthens, the resent history itself grows — explaining rising per-call token volume, latency, and cost with no change in response length.

whyWrong.A: A fifty-turn conversation is far below any context-window limit; exceeding it cannot explain a steady rise from this early stage.
whyWrong.B: Claude's API is stateless and keeps no memory buffer between calls; nothing about the model's internals accumulates across turns at all.
whyWrong.C: The stem states each response stays about the same length, which rules out response length as the driver of the rising cost.

t1Clause: even though each response stays about the same length

stem: Three teams each pasted a shared safety-guardrail clause from a wiki page into their own system prompts. After security tightens the wording, two teams still run the outdated version, weeks ahead of next quarter's security audit. What should the platform team do?

opts.t: Consolidate the guardrail into one versioned, shared component that every team references, so an edit is one reviewable change.
Post the tightened wording on the wiki again and ask each team to re-copy it before the audit.
Let each team keep customizing its own copy for flexibility, since minor wording differences rarely matter.
Have security audit each team's system prompt quarterly and flag any outdated guardrail wording found.

whyRight: A single versioned, shared component every team references turns a guardrail edit into one reviewable event, closing the gap that already left two teams running outdated wording ahead of the security audit. A wiki page or per-team copies cannot stay synchronized once any side edits independently.

whyWrong.B: Re-posting the wording once more repeats the exact copy-paste pattern that already produced two outdated teams; nothing keeps future copies synchronized after this update.
whyWrong.C: Treating wording drift as harmless is the exact pattern that already left two teams outdated ahead of the audit; flexibility here means silent, unmonitored divergence.
whyWrong.D: Quarterly auditing finds outdated wording after teams have already drifted; it doesn't remove the root cause of maintaining separate pasted copies in the first place.

t1Clause: two teams still run the outdated version

stem: Team policy ties reasoning-cue use to task shape: multi-step tasks get a chain-of-thought cue, single-step tasks don't. A workflow already applies the cue while comparing findings across six audit reports. Finance proposes removing it to cut token cost. What should the team do?

opts.t: Keep the cue; comparing six audit reports is genuinely multi-step, and removing it would cost the deliberation accuracy depends on.
Remove the cue entirely to capture the projected cost cut, since trimming prompt overhead is safe wherever possible.
Replace the cue with several few-shot examples of correct rankings, to protect accuracy while cutting token overhead.
Keep the cue only for the highest-risk report and drop it for the rest, splitting the cost saving.

whyRight: Team policy ties cue use to task shape, and a six-report comparison is genuinely multi-step, so the cue is already correctly applied. Removing it to save tokens breaks the very policy that put it there, discarding the deliberation the task's accuracy depends on.

whyWrong.B: Removing the cue is what policy calls for only on single-step tasks; here it strips deliberation a six-report comparison needs, trading accuracy for a saving the task can't safely absorb.
whyWrong.C: Few-shot examples fix output-format consistency, not the deliberation a multi-step ranking across six reports requires; swapping techniques addresses the wrong axis of the problem entirely.
whyWrong.D: Splitting the cue across reports leaves five of six comparisons without the deliberation the task's own complexity requires, undermining the accuracy the cue exists to protect.

t1Clause: comparing findings across six audit reports
lessonKey: accuracy audit comparing cost cue deliberation depends genuinely keep multi removing reports six step would

stem: Team policy reserves hybrid fact-extraction for conversations with precision-critical details; others get plain summarization. A brainstorming session with no dosages, IDs, or amounts must stay under a strict compression-latency ceiling. An engineer proposes hybrid extraction anyway, 'to be safe.' What should the team do?

opts.t: Apply hybrid extraction anyway, since treating every session as potentially precision-critical is the more cautious default.
Apply hybrid extraction but drop the verbatim recent-turns portion to offset the added latency it introduces.
Keep only the most recent portion of the conversation to fit the latency ceiling, discarding everything earlier.
Use plain summarization; the session has no precision-critical facts, so hybrid extraction adds overhead for no accuracy benefit.

whyRight: The session contains no precision-critical facts, so nothing needs verbatim extraction; hybrid extraction's structured-block step is pure overhead here. Under a strict compression-latency ceiling, plain summarization satisfies the requirement directly, while the more elaborate technique burns the latency budget for no accuracy gain.

whyWrong.A: Treating every session as potentially precision-critical ignores the stated fact that this one has none; the extra extraction step only spends latency budget the ceiling doesn't allow.
whyWrong.B: Dropping the verbatim-turns step still leaves the unneeded structured-extraction overhead in place; the session never had facts requiring that step to begin with.
whyWrong.C: Discarding earlier turns entirely is unnecessary here; nothing precision-critical was ever at risk, and plain summarization already fits the ceiling without losing content wholesale.

lessonKey: accuracy adds benefit critical extraction facts has hybrid overhead plain precision session so summarization use

stem: Compliance requires an audit stamp on every request; the same policy preamble is also sent every call to enable caching under a latency and cost SLA. An engineer wants the stamp positioned before the preamble, breaking the cached prefix. What should the team do?

opts.t: Drop the audit stamp from cached requests, relying on a separate compliance log to record disclosure after the fact.
Keep the policy preamble first for a stable prefix, and place the audit stamp after it on every request.
Place the audit stamp before the policy preamble on every call, guaranteeing compliance even though the prefix now varies.
Split the policy preamble into two shorter blocks so the stamp can sit between them without affecting caching.

whyRight: Keeping the unchanging policy preamble first preserves the byte-identical prefix caching needs, satisfying the SLA, while placing the audit stamp right after it still delivers the stamp on every single request, satisfying compliance. Both requirements hold without forcing either into the other's way.

whyWrong.A: Dropping the stamp from the actual request breaks the compliance requirement outright; a separate log records that disclosure happened elsewhere, not that this request carried it.
whyWrong.C: The stem already states this placement varies the prefix on every call, which the caching requirement depends on staying identical; the SLA fails the moment the prefix changes.
whyWrong.D: Splitting the preamble into two blocks abandons the single stable prefix caching reuses; the SLA still isn't met even though the stamp now sits between them.

t1Clause: the same policy preamble is also sent every call to enable caching under a latency and cost SLA
lessonKey: after audit every first keep place policy preamble prefix request stable stamp
